jobs.text: For a document Q&A assistant for an education team, my closest prior work is an education voice-intent classifier delivered in 2025 that used Airflow-scheduled NLP classification and improved the client’s key metric by 9% [E1]. That system included nightly DAGs for retraining and publishing the model over noisy support tickets, with chained prompts and output parsers [E2]. For retrieval, I have managed a similarity-search index with metadata filters using Pinecone in a contract summariser [E6]. For computer vision, I built CV models in travel churn and fintech voice-intent projects [E3][E4].

Your logistics team needs a recommendation engine whose suggestions dispatchers accept, not just a technically correct model. Direct logistics case studies are not in my evidence, so I would not claim that as a core strength. The same orchestration and scheduling stack, however, appears in adjacent work. In an energy voice-intent classifier, I used LangChain to chain prompts, tools, and output parsers and nightly DAGs to retrain and publish the model, delivering a 15% improvement in the client’s key metric [E1][E2]. In an education NLP classifier, Airflow scheduled the system and LangChain orchestrated it, improving the key metric by 9% [E3][E4]. For a logistics recommendation engine, I would first define acceptance rate as the primary metric and log accept/reject outcomes. LangChain can coordinate candidate retrieval, score explanation, and structured output [E1][E2]. Airflow DAGs can retrain nightly on those outcomes and republish the model, as done in the energy and education projects [E1][E3][E4]. Model and prompt choices can be tuned against acceptance rate using the Bayesian search approach from the energy project [E1].

Your manufacturing churn predictor needs containerized retraining, API serving, and scheduled orchestration. The closest documented analogue is an education churn predictor where I managed training jobs and endpoints and shipped reproducible Docker images to the client’s cluster [E1]. This was not a manufacturing client, but the deployment pattern transfers to manufacturing support or maintenance signals. For serving, I have delivered FastAPI endpoints for demand and price models [E3][E4]. For orchestration, I have built nightly Airflow DAGs that retrain and publish an NLP classification system over noisy support tickets [E5][E6], which is directly relevant to churn signals from support interactions. On modeling, I have used gradient boosting with XGBoost and parameter-efficient adapters on a 7B model [E4].

The closest direct evidence is a contract summariser I built for a media client using Pinecone and AWS SageMaker [E3]. In that project, I managed a similarity-search index with metadata filters and ran pipelines of imputers, scalers, and random forests with cross-validation [E3]. For orchestration, I have built Airflow DAGs that retrain and publish NLP models on a nightly schedule [E1][E2]. I do not have a retail-specific case study for contract summarisation, so I will not claim one. The media project transfers to retail because contract metadata such as suppliers, dates, and categories can be handled by the same Pinecone metadata-filtered similarity search [E3]. SageMaker managed training jobs and endpoints would support summarisation models at retail volumes, as I have used in previous deployments [E5]. Airflow scheduling would apply the same nightly retraining pattern to keep summaries current [E1][E2].

I have not delivered a recommendation engine for a retail client; the closest is a fintech recommendation engine [E2]. That system combined boosted trees tuned with Bayesian search and parameter-efficient adapters on a 7B model, and logged every experiment's parameters and artifacts to a registry with MLflow [E2]. For MLflow, I also tracked runs in a media price optimiser and logged experiment parameters and artifacts to a registry [E1][E2]. For NLP, I built text classification over noisy support tickets in a media fraud scorer, yielding a 32% improvement in the client's key metric [E3], and a media price optimiser with a 9% improvement [E1]. I built an education voice-intent classifier with a 9% improvement [E4]. These systems are transferable to retail: product descriptions, reviews, and customer queries are text inputs similar to the noisy tickets and voice intents I classified [E1][E3][E4], while MLflow experiment tracking from the fintech engine supports ranking model selection [E2].

I can point to OAuth and real-time push experience: a logistics inventory tracker delivered in 2026 used third-party sign-in with token refresh and scopes, and pushed order status updates to open browsers [E1][E2]. Playwright appears in a retail inventory tracker with browser end-to-end regression tests and subscription billing via webhooks [E5][E6]. I would treat those as gaps rather than claim unsupported experience.

I do not have a direct manufacturing client example, so I will map relevant adjacent work rather than claim manufacturing experience. For OAuth-controlled access, an energy marketplace storefront used OAuth login with Redis caching and delivered a 35% improvement in the client's key metric [E2]; a logistics inventory tracker used OAuth login with real-time order status and achieved a 36% improvement [E6]. Redis caching also supported a fintech order-tracking app with a 12% improvement [E1] and a retail inventory tracker with Celery workers and a 45% improvement [E3]. Celery handled background email and report generation in a travel admin dashboard [E4]. In a manufacturing portal, these map to controlled supplier or customer sign-in, cached order and inventory status, and scheduled report or document jobs. The outcomes are from adjacent operations settings, but the mechanisms transfer to manufacturing workflows.

I have built GraphQL APIs for subscription billing and checkout in a retail tracker [E2], and delivered a Django education admin dashboard on AWS with third-party sign-in, token refresh, scopes, and Docker deployment, where the client saw a 17% improvement in their key metric [E3][E4]. For real-time updates, I have used WebSockets on event-loop JavaScript backend services in a real estate portal and a fintech order-tracking app [E5][E6].

A healthcare learning portal needs reliable background tasks, secure sign-in, server-rendered pages, and live updates. For Celery, I used background task queues for emails and report generation [E2] and Celery workers in a retail inventory tracker that produced a 45% improvement in the client’s key metric [E1]. For OAuth, I implemented third-party sign-in with token refresh and scopes [E3][E5][E6]. For Next.js, I used the App Router with server-rendered pages and file-based routing [E5][E6]. I can bring these patterns to your portal, with the caveat that healthcare-specific compliance or clinical workflow experience is not a core strength I can evidence here.

Your travel team’s marketplace storefront will need reliable checkout flows, a solid database layer, and cloud-ready deployment. My closest past work is a retail booking platform using PostgreSQL and a Django backend [E3]. For browser-critical storefront behavior, I have built Playwright end-to-end regression suites in CI for a retail inventory tracker that also handled card checkout, webhooks, and subscription billing [E1][E2]. For infrastructure, I have used Docker to containerise services in a fintech admin dashboard [E5] and deployed an education admin dashboard on AWS with Docker [E6]. I also have no travel-client engagement to cite; the closest domain match is the retail booking platform [E3]. I can bring that database, testing, and deployment experience to a travel storefront, but travel-specific requirements would be new ground.

Your travel team needs a client portal with reliable checkout, background processing, and test coverage. I can build that from direct travel work and adjacent portal work. For a travel marketplace storefront, I implemented Stripe payments, OAuth login, Docker deployment, and caching/rate limiting, with a 32% improvement in the client's key metric [E4]. In a travel admin dashboard, I ran Celery through Django for background tasks such as email and report generation [E5]. Those two requirements are already grounded in travel projects. For Playwright, I built a browser end-to-end regression suite in CI for a retail inventory tracker that also used Celery workers [E1][E2]. GraphQL is not from travel either: I delivered GraphQL APIs for a manufacturing client portal and a retail inventory tracker [E6][E2]. I would apply those same schema and query patterns to this portal rather than claiming they were already applied in travel.

For a travel pricing analysis, the required toolchain is directly covered by my listed skill set: SQL, BigQuery, dbt, Tableau, and A/B testing [E2]. My CV records 22 delivered projects including travel engagements, but the case evidence I can cite here does not include a travel-specific pricing study; I would treat that as a gap rather than overstate it [E2]. Adjacent work includes BigQuery event-log analysis with randomised experiment design and significance/power checks [E3], dbt transformations with versioning and testing over the warehouse [E5], and Tableau dashboards with data cleaning and Python automation [E1]. That combination supports pricing analysis through experiment design for price tests and dashboards for pricing metrics. I can apply those methods to your travel data without claiming a prior travel pricing case.

For your travel team's cohort retention study, the core stack I would apply is BigQuery for event-level retention queries, SQL for window functions and CTEs over multi-million-row tables [E3][E4], Python for dataframe wrangling and reshaping [E3][E5][E6], Excel for summary delivery [E4], and Airflow for scheduled pipeline runs [E4]. I have used BigQuery in serverless warehouse querying over event logs [E1][E2]. On travel

Your fintech segmentation study depends on scheduled data pipelines and clean customer records. I have built dependency-aware nightly Airflow schedules for healthcare and manufacturing reporting [E1][E3]. For analytical work with similar table operations, I have used window functions and CTEs over multi-million-row tables in healthcare survey analysis [E1] and travel finance forecasting [E4]. I also deduplicated and fixed inconsistent customer records for a manufacturing KPI suite [E3]. In an energy engagement, Airflow-orchestrated reporting contributed to a 19% improvement in the client's key metric [E2]. I have not completed a segmentation study for a fintech client

Your fintech project is a close match for the work described below. For Power BI, I applied it in my Manufacturing KPI reporting suite project [E1]. For forecasting, I applied it in my Travel finance close model (repo) project [E3]. I would be glad to walk you through the approach and a sensible first milestone.

In 2021 I delivered a manufacturing KPI reporting suite using Looker explores, with deduplication and fixing inconsistent customer records, orchestrated in Airflow [E1]. In 2022 I delivered a media customer segmentation study using Tableau dashboards, data cleaning, Python automation, and window functions over multi-million-row tables [E3]. The closest client context in my evidence is manufacturing, not logistics, so I would not claim direct logistics domain experience. The transferable pieces for a close model are cleaning inconsistent records, automating reporting workflows, and building drill-down dashboards for close review [E1][E4]. Looker explores could support governed metric access for close metrics, while Tableau dashboards could support drill-down review [E1][E4]. I can describe how those steps would apply to a finance close model, but I cannot cite a logistics-specific case from my history.

Your education team’s marketing attribution report needs clean event data, dependable orchestration, and sound statistical measurement. This delivered a 37% improvement in the client’s key metric [E3][E4]. That statistical and data preparation work maps directly to attribution modeling. For Airflow, I scheduled dependency-aware nightly pipelines and built a versioned transformation layer in a healthcare survey analysis [E1], and used Airflow for statistical KPI reporting in an energy project [E2]. Those patterns transfer to loading education marketing touchpoints and refreshing attribution outputs. For data cleaning, I performed deduplication and correction of inconsistent customer records in a media segmentation study, along with Python dataframe wrangling [E5][E6]; the same approach applies to cleaning marketing identifiers in education data.

For your education team’s warehouse migration, my closest project is an education warehouse migration where I built ETL pipelines, modelled in dbt, and deduplicated and fixed inconsistent customer records in BigQuery; the cloud warehouse was configured with role-based access and clustering, and the client saw a 38% improvement in their key metric [E1]. The ETL work included cleaning duplicate customer records before loading into the warehouse, which is directly relevant to migration quality [E1]. For orchestration, I have used Airflow to run dependency-aware nightly pipeline schedules in a healthcare survey analysis project and in a manufacturing KPI reporting suite [E5][E3]. I can describe the migration steps, data validation, and scheduling approach in more detail if helpful.
